common_name: Variegatus Japanese Sweet Flag (White-Striped Sweet Flag)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in consistently moist to wet soil; in zone 9 plant September-April. Variegatus tolerates more sun than the golden Ogon cultivar but still performs best in partial shade in the hot Gulf South.

directions: Plant in partial shade to full shade in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Variegatus tolerates shallow standing water and thrives at pond margins and bog gardens. This is the classic white-and-green striped cultivar of Japanese sweet flag, producing narrow, grass-like, fan-shaped clumps of leaves cleanly edged and striped in creamy white, giving a crisp, cool color accent that reads well against darker-leaved shade companions. Unlike true grasses, Acorus is an iris relative that spreads slowly by rhizome to form a dense, low, evergreen mat useful as edging along a shaded path or pond, or as a textural container plant. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, and keep soil from drying out, since this cultivar declines quickly in dry conditions.

planting.note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 8-9 plant March-April. Portadora is root-hardy in zone 8b-11 with heavy winter mulch; farther north lift and store tubers indoors over winter.

directions: Plant in rich, moist to boggy soil in partial shade to full sun with consistent irrigation; Portadora is among the largest commonly grown elephant ears, producing enormous, ruffled-edged, blue-green leaves on thick upright petioles that can top eight feet in a single season under good conditions, making it one of the fastest and boldest ways to create an instant tropical canopy. Its scale and vigor suit it to large borders, pondside plantings, and screening rather than small containers, where its size quickly overwhelms companion plants. Feed heavily and keep soil consistently moist to wet through the growing season for maximum leaf size, since the plant naturally grows in marshy, waterlogged ground. Where winters bring hard freezes, dig and store the large tubers dry and frost-free until spring, or in zone 8b and warmer simply mulch heavily and let the root-hardy tuber resprout.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Colocasia Cultivars for Florida

common_name: Black Lava Elephant Ear (Glossy Near-Black Colocasia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 8-9 plant March-April. Black Lava is root-hardy in zone 8b-11 with heavy winter mulch; farther north lift and store tubers indoors over winter.

directions: Plant in rich, moist soil in partial shade to full sun with consistent moisture; Black Lava produces glossy, deep purple-black leaves so dark they read as true black in most garden light, held on matching near-black stems for a dramatic, uniformly dark presence unlike the mottled or veined patterns of many other dark colocasia cultivars. The smooth, high-gloss leaf surface catches and reflects light, keeping the deep color from reading flat, and the strong color contrast makes it a striking companion to chartreuse or silver-leaved plants nearby. Feed regularly and keep soil consistently moist to wet for the best leaf size and darkest color, since color can fade to a more muted purple-green in drier or leaner conditions. Where winters bring hard freezes, dig and store the tubers dry and frost-free, or in zone 8b and warmer mulch heavily and let the root-hardy tuber resprout in spring.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Colocasia Cultivars for Florida

common_name: Super Ellen Crinum (Burgundy-Leaved Pink Crinum Lily)

planting.note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Super Ellen is a selection prized for deep burgundy-purple strap foliage in addition to its flowers.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Super Ellen is a selection related to the classic Ellen Bosanquet crinum, distinguished by broad strap-like leaves that emerge in a rich burgundy-purple and hold good color through the season, giving the clump ornamental value even between bloom cycles, topped with clusters of fragrant pink to wine-pink trumpet flowers on tall sturdy scapes through the warm months. Like other crinums, the large bulb persists and slowly multiplies for decades with minimal care once established, tolerating heat, humidity, and a range of soils with ease. Division is rarely needed, since crinum bulbs bloom best when left undisturbed and slightly crowded; simply remove spent flower stalks and any winter-damaged foliage.
